author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts health officials have confirmed the state’s 13th human case of West Nile virus this year, extending a late-season run of mosquito-borne disease activity. The Massachusetts Department of Public Health said in its Oct. 9 [announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/state-health-officials-announce-13th-human-case-of-west-nile-virus-in-massachusetts) that the patient is a woman in her 40s who was likely exposed in Middlesex County. [The Boston Globe independently reported the case and the state’s risk designations](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/09/metro/mass-health-officials-confirm-13th-human-case-west-nile-virus-woman-exposed-middlesex-county/).

The case count is statewide, but the highest current risk designations are concentrated in 11 communities: Boston, Brookline, Cambridge, Chelsea, Everett, Malden, Newton, Revere, Somerville, Watertown and Winthrop. DPH says most of the rest of Massachusetts remains at moderate risk. The designations are public-health warnings based on surveillance and exposure patterns; they do not mean that every mosquito in a listed community carries the virus or that every outdoor location presents the same danger.

The latest patient was likely exposed in Middlesex County, an area that has appeared repeatedly in the state’s human-case and mosquito-surveillance updates. DPH does not identify individual patients in the announcement, and the release does not describe the woman’s symptoms, treatment or current condition. Those details remain unknown. The confirmed facts are the diagnosis, the likely county of exposure and the resulting statewide total of 13 human cases this year.

Mosquito testing shows why officials continue to describe the season as active. DPH said the first West Nile-positive mosquitoes of 2026 were announced June 16 and that 344 samples had tested positive by Oct. 9 across 13 counties: Barnstable, Berkshire, Bristol, Dukes, Essex, Franklin, Hampden, Hampshire, Middlesex, Norfolk, Plymouth, Suffolk and Worcester. A positive mosquito sample is a surveillance finding, not an additional human case, so the sample count and human-case count should not be combined.

The state is also tracking Eastern equine encephalitis, or EEE, a separate mosquito-borne virus. The Oct. 9 update listed 27 EEE-positive mosquito samples, with no human or animal EEE cases reported so far this year. DPH also reported no animal cases of West Nile virus. Keeping those categories separate matters for readers comparing the numbers: mosquito detections help public-health officials map activity, while human and animal cases describe illness in people or other hosts.

The timing matters because Massachusetts’ mosquito season is not over simply because temperatures are cooling. DPH says West Nile risk will continue until the first hard frost. For residents in high-risk communities, that means evening and early-morning outdoor activities can still bring exposure, particularly when mosquitoes are most active. The state’s daily [Massachusetts Arbovirus Update](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-arbovirus-update) page is the appropriate place to check for changing risk levels and new surveillance results.

The department recommends using an EPA-registered insect repellent as directed, wearing long sleeves, long pants and socks when outdoors, and considering whether activities can be moved away from dusk and dawn. People can also limit mosquito breeding around their homes by draining standing water, checking gutters and drains, emptying unused containers and changing birdbath water frequently. Tight-fitting screens provide another layer of protection indoors.

The precautions apply across the state, but the high-risk list gives communities a more specific signal about where officials see the greatest concern right now. Residents should not infer that a moderate designation means no risk, or that a high designation makes outdoor activity impossible. It means people should use the available protections consistently while surveillance continues. Animal owners should remove standing water and ask a veterinarian about approved mosquito precautions and vaccines for horses, DPH said.

For Massachusetts, the new case is both a public-health update and a reminder that the season’s risk map can change after summer has ended. The state has not reported a human EEE case or an animal West Nile case this year, but the continued mosquito detections and the 13 human West Nile cases support the department’s advice to keep prevention measures in place until a hard frost ends the season.
dek: A woman in her 40s was likely exposed in Middlesex County as Massachusetts keeps 11 communities at high risk for West Nile virus and continues mosquito surveillance.
headline: Massachusetts confirms 13th human West Nile case as fall risk continues
seoDescription: Massachusetts confirms its 13th human West Nile case of 2026 as 11 communities remain at high risk and mosquito surveillance continues.
seoTitle: Massachusetts confirms 13th human West Nile case
